message.content: Read redu.md and deploy Filestash on redu.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.
- aws-billing-and-cost-management: Analyze AWS costs, find savings, manage budgets, evaluate Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, right-size EC2/Lambda/RDS/EBS with Compute Optimizer, look up service pricing, query CUR with Athena, detect cost anomalies, scope costs to billing views, and monitor Free Tier usage. Triggers on: AWS bill, cost analysis, reduce spend, savings plan, reserved instance, right-size, budget alert, cost optimization, pricing, free tier, cost anomaly, CUR, cost audit, billing view, billing view ARN.
- aws-blocks: Guides building full-stack applications with AWS Blocks — an Infrastructure-from-Code framework. Applies when creating APIs, selecting Building Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, Database, AuthBasic, AuthCognito, Realtime, AsyncJob, FileBucket, etc.), running local development, or deploying AWS Blocks applications. Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Triggers when user mentions AWS Blocks; project has aws-blocks/ directory; code imports @aws-blocks packages.
- aws-cdk: Authors, deploys, and troubleshoots AWS infrastructure using CDK with TypeScript or Python. Covers best practices, stack architecture, and construct patterns. Always use when writing CDK constructs, bootstrapping environments, running cdk deploy/synth/diff, fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors, planning stack structure, importing existing resources, resolving drift, or refactoring stacks without resource replacement.
- aws-cloudformation: Author, validate, and troubleshoot AWS CloudFormation templates. Covers template authoring with secure defaults, pre-deployment validation (cfn-lint, cfn-guard, change sets), and root-cause diagnosis of failed stacks using CloudFormation events and CloudTrail correlation.
- aws-containers: Deploys and operates containerized workloads on ECS, Fargate, and ECR. Covers task definitions, Fargate services, ECR repository setup and lifecycle policies, ECS Exec debugging, service scaling, deployment strategies, load balancer integration, and logging configuration. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.
- aws-messaging-and-streaming: Guides use of AWS messaging and streaming services. Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.
- aws-sdk-js-v3-usage: AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 development patterns. Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.
- aws-sdk-swift-usage: AWS SDK for Swift development patterns. Use when writing Swift code that uses AWS services via aws-sdk-swift package.
- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Covers cold starts, CORS debugging, event source mappings, troubleshooting, concurrency, SnapStart, Powertools, function URLs, EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda layers, and production readiness. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." Does not apply to EC2, ECS/Fargate containers, or Amplify hosting.
- cso: Chief Security Officer mode. (gstack)
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- investigate: Systematic debugging with root cause investigation. (gstack)
- office-hours: YC Office Hours — two modes. (gstack)
- review: Pre-landing PR review. (gstack)
- signing-in-to-aws: Gets AWS credentials for CLI/SDK access via `aws login`. Activates when a developer needs to authenticate to AWS for local development, when an AWS operation fails due to missing or expired credentials, or when someone asks about setting up AWS access. Triggers: "set up AWS", "configure AWS", "aws login", "get credentials", "authenticate", "session expired", "token expired", "no credentials", "AccessDeniedException" with no configured credentials.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.content:
---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/mickael-kerjean/filestash
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: machines/filestash pinned by digest (there are no version tags)
  port: 8334
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: none. Filestash keeps its own state in SQLite files on a volume, and the FILES live on whatever storage you point it at.
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0278
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: filestash
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: NOBODY, UNLESS YOU SET ADMIN_PASSWORD, AND UNTIL YOU DO, EVERY ANONYMOUS REQUEST IS ALREADY AN ADMIN. This is the reason this entry exists in the shape it does, so read it before anything else. server/middleware/session.go:29-56, the AdminOnly middleware, wraps its ENTIRE check in an if statement that only runs when auth.admin is non-empty. With no admin password the middleware calls the handler with no check at all, and routes.go:40-47 puts GET /admin/api/config, POST /admin/api/config, the workflow CRUD and the audit log behind exactly that middleware. So on a fresh instance anyone can READ the whole configuration, including the secret key and any stored credentials, and WRITE it, including setting the admin password to their own. server/ctrl/admin.go:16-20 confirms it from the other side: GET /admin/api/session returns true when auth.admin is empty. And static.go:49,80 redirects every page to the setup form, so the app actively shows a stranger the door. There is no wizard token and no first-visitor lock. ADMIN_PASSWORD is the ONLY thing that closes this, and cmd/main.go:26-46 applies it during InitConfig, several steps before the listener binds. NEVER deploy this without it."
  - "⛔⛔ ADMIN_PASSWORD MUST CONTAIN A BCRYPT HASH, NOT A PASSWORD, AND GETTING IT WRONG LOCKS YOU OUT FOREVER WITH NO ERROR. config.go:242-246 stores the environment value verbatim through ConfigElement.Set (:429-444), which does no hashing; the hashing normally happens in the BROWSER at public/assets/pages/adminpage/ctrl_setup.js:91. Every login then runs bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword against the stored string. Put a plaintext password in and the comparison can never succeed, while auth.admin is non-empty so the setup page is gone and the admin console is unreachable by anybody including you. Upstream asserts the same rule in its own health check: server/ctrl/report.go:73-75 flags the config when auth.admin is not exactly 60 characters, which is the length of a bcrypt hash. Generate one, for example with a throwaway container: run htpasswd -bnBC 12 with an empty username inside httpd:2.4-alpine and strip the leading colon and the newline. golang.org/x/crypto v0.54.0 bcrypt.go:265-279 accepts $2a$, $2b$ and $2y$ alike, so an htpasswd hash is fine. THEN PROVE IT: the /healthz check below tells you the length is right, and signing in proves the password matches. Do both."
  - "⛔⛔ CLOSE THE FRONT DOOR TOO, AND DO IT AS THE FIRST STEP AFTER BOOT. ADMIN_PASSWORD settles who owns the admin console; it does nothing about the connect form on the home page. middleware.identity_provider.type defaults to EMPTY (server/ctrl/session.go:192-203), and config/config.json ships seven connectors: WebDav, FTP, SFTP, GIT, S3, Dropbox and Drive. So an anonymous visitor cannot read YOUR files, they have no credentials, but they can make YOUR server open outbound connections to any host they name. That is an SSRF probe into the user's own private network and a free egress relay, and it is the same class of problem that got changedetection.io dropped from this library. The fix is upstream's own admin authentication plugin (server/plugin/plg_authenticate_admin/index.go), which redirects visitors to a password page where only the admin password is accepted. Set middleware.identity_provider.type to admin through POST /admin/api/config immediately after the container is healthy, BEFORE you hand the URL over, and verify it with the anonymous check below. If the user wants a genuinely public file browser, that is a decision to take with them, not a default to leave in place."
  - "⛔ EVERY SCRIPTED CALL TO THE ADMIN API NEEDS THE HEADER X-Requested-With: XmlHttpRequest, AND WITHOUT IT THE FAILURE LOOKS LIKE AN AUTH FAILURE. server/middleware/http.go:94-100, inside SecureOrigin, lets a request through only when that header is present, or when features.api.enable is true AND the request carries no cookies; otherwise it logs Intrusion detection and returns ErrNotAllowed. routes.go:35-47 puts the whole admin API behind SecureOrigin. So a plain curl to /admin/api/session gets refused, which reads exactly like a wrong password and will send you hunting the bcrypt hash instead of the header. Add the header to every admin call, and gate your script on a well-formed response body rather than on a status code."
  - "⛔ DO NOT WRITE A CHECK AGAINST /admin/api/session, BECAUSE ITS HEALTHY ANSWER IS AN ABSENCE. server/common/response.go:13-16 tags the field as Result interface{} with json:\"result,omitempty\", so SendSuccessResult(res, false) encodes to a body with NO result key at all. The correctly-locked instance therefore answers {status: ok} and nothing else, which is indistinguishable from a request that was refused before it reached the handler. A script that reads 'no result: true present' as a pass would pass on a 502, on a missing header, and on a typo in the hostname. Probe GET /admin/api/config instead: it has three outcomes that can be told apart, a result key means the config came back and the instance is OPEN, Permission Denied means AdminOnly refused you which is what you want, and Not Allowed means SecureOrigin refused you so the test never ran. Both refusals are HTTP 403, so it is the MESSAGE that distinguishes them (server/common/error.go:17-18)."
  - "⛔ APPLICATION_URL MUST BE EXACTLY THE PUBLIC HOSTNAME, AND SETTING IT WRONG BREAKS EVERYTHING EXCEPT /admin. config.go:247-250 maps it onto general.host, and SecureOrigin (http.go:81-92) then refuses any request whose Host header does not match, with the single exception of paths starting /admin/. That exception is a kindness, not a bug: it is how you get back in and fix it. Generate the dname yourself UP FRONT in full filestash-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form and pass that; a bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match. The value is the bare host, no scheme."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE wopi_server SERVICE. Upstream's compose runs collabora/code beside the app, and on redu it is all cost and no benefit: it is an entire LibreOffice, many times the size of Filestash itself, it publishes port 9980, it runs as user: root, its aliasgroup1 is the wildcard https://.*:443, and its command curls a stylesheet from a third-party GitHub gist on EVERY start, which is both a boot-time dependency on somebody else's server and a supply-chain hook. Drop it and leave OFFICE_URL unset: plg_editor_wopi/config.go:10-24 defaults features.office.enable to FALSE unless OFFICE_URL is set, so this is a clean disable rather than a break. What you lose is in-browser editing of Word, Excel and PowerPoint documents. Everything else, including browsing, uploading, downloading, image and video preview, and the text and code editors, is unaffected. If a user genuinely needs office editing, that is a second VM sized for LibreOffice, not a container squeezed onto this one."
  - "⛔ THERE IS NO VERSION TO PIN, SO PIN THE DIGEST. The Docker Hub repository machines/filestash carries 310 tags and not one of them is a version: the only current tag is latest, rebuilt 2026-08-16, and the rest are 2023-era git shas plus the oddities lowa, trial and a latest-amd64 from 2025-06-30. GitHub publishes no releases either. So reaching for the rolling tag is not laziness here, it is the only tag there is, which is exactly why it must not go in a recipe: it moves under you and a redeploy silently crosses however many months of changes. Pin machines/filestash@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:22fabc40», which was the latest manifest on 2026-08-17. Upgrading means reading the new digest yourself and deciding to move; there is no changelog to read first, so treat an upgrade as a change with a rollback plan."
  - "⛔ MOUNT A VOLUME ON /app/data/state/ OR EVERY REDEPLOY IS A FACTORY RESET. This is the whole product state: constants.go:20-26 puts config under state/config (including the admin hash, the secret key and any configured connections), certificates under state/certs, plugins under state/plugins, SQLite databases under state/db, the search index under state/search and logs under state/log. server/model/index.go:15 and four widget plugins open SQLite files in state/db for share links, workflows, metadata, chat and recents. This is NOT the silent-SQLite-fallback trap the rest of this library warns about: Filestash has no other mode, the SQLite is deliberate, and the volume IS the answer. ⚠️ Note that TMP_PATH is cache/, OUTSIDE state/, and constants.go:53 wipes it at boot, which is correct and is why it is not on the volume. Use a NAMED volume rather than a bind mount into the project directory, because a source re-upload replaces that directory. A fresh named volume is seeded from the image, which already ships a default config.json and is chowned to the filestash user by docker/Dockerfile:37, so there is no permission dance."
  - "THE SECRET THAT A REDEPLOY DESTROYS IS general.secret_key, AND THERE IS NO ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE FOR IT. config.go:251-255 generates it as a 16-character random string on first boot and writes it into config.json, and constants.go:71-77 derives the admin cookie key, the user session key, the hash key and the signature key from it. Lose it and every admin session, every user session and every share-link proof stops verifying; anything encrypted in the config stops decrypting. Because it lives in the config file rather than the environment, THE VOLUME IS THE THING YOU PROTECT, which is the same sentence as the quirk above and is why that one is not optional. There is a related variable, CONFIG_SECRET: [REDACTED:value] it and the encrypted config paths (the identity-provider and attribute-mapping params) are keyed from it instead of from general.secret_key (config_state.go:43-47,84). Setting it means one fewer thing living only on the volume; changing it later makes those two fields undecryptable. Decide once."
  - "⛔ DO NOT PUT STORAGE CREDENTIALS INTO A PRE-CONFIGURED CONNECTION. THAT ARRAY IS SERVED TO ANONYMOUS CALLERS. config.go:318 Export() puts this.Conn into the payload verbatim with no redaction, and routes.go:96 serves that payload at GET /api/config with PublicCORS and no authentication middleware. The seven default connectors carry only a type and a label, so a stock instance leaks nothing. But the admin console lets you pre-fill a connection with a hostname, a username and a password so users do not have to type them, and anything you put there is world-readable at that URL. Let each user supply their own credentials at the login form, which is the design Filestash is actually built around."
  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST REACHES ONCE THE TWO STEPS ABOVE ARE DONE: the password page from the admin authentication plugin, GET /healthz, GET /about, GET /api/config (the public config), GET /api/backend (the shape of each connector's login form), GET /api/plugin, the static assets, robots.txt, manifest.json, /.well-known/security.txt, and any share links the user has deliberately created under /s/<share>. GET /admin/api/session still answers anonymously, by design, but with an admin password set it answers false rather than true. No file, no directory listing, no configuration write."
  - "NO DATABASE, AND THAT IS NOT AN OVERSIGHT. Do not attach a managed Postgres: Filestash stores its own state in SQLite on the volume and the actual FILES live on whatever remote storage the user connects to, which is the entire point of the product. lib/pq and go-sql-driver/mysql are in go.mod because Postgres and MySQL are browsable BACKENDS, not because Filestash needs one. So redu's one-database-per-managed-Postgres rule does not apply here at all, and there is no db_extensions, no db_superuser and no migrate_command."

# Self-host Filestash on redu

One web file manager in front of all your storage: SFTP, FTP, S3, WebDAV, Git, Dropbox, Google
Drive. One small Go container, a volume, a public HTTPS URL, and no database at all.

## What this deploys

- **Filestash** from the official image, pinned by digest, on one m1.medium VM, port 8334.
- A named volume on `/app/data/state/`, which holds the configuration, the signing secret and
  the SQLite files behind share links and search.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
- **No database.** Filestash keeps its own state on the volume, and your files stay where they
  already are.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Filestash on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Read this part before you deploy it anywhere

A **stock Filestash is an unauthenticated admin console.** That is not a bug report, it is what the
code says: the middleware that guards the admin API wraps its entire check inside "if an admin
password is set". With no admin password, an anonymous request can read the whole configuration and
write it back, including setting the admin password to its own.

Filestash is in this library, and changedetection.io was researched and dropped, for one reason:
Filestash has an environment variable that closes this **before the process ever listens.** So this
recipe is built around two steps that are not optional:

1. **`ADMIN_PASSWORD` at deploy time**, which settles who owns the console.
2. **The admin authentication middleware, set the moment the container is healthy**, which settles
   who can reach the connect form at all.

Without the second one, an anonymous visitor cannot read your files, but they can make your server
open outbound connections to any host they name, which is a probe into your own private network and
a free relay out of it.

## The password is a hash, not a password

This one has cost people their instance. `ADMIN_PASSWORD` is stored **verbatim** and compared
with `bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword`. Filestash normally hashes in the browser, on the setup page.
So the variable must contain a **bcrypt hash**, and a plaintext password produces an instance that
nobody, including you, can ever administer: the comparison can never match, and because the value
is non-empty the setup page is gone.

Upstream agrees, in its own health check, which flags the config whenever the stored value is not
exactly 60 characters. That is the length of a bcrypt hash.

```bash
# Generate one without installing anything. Keep BOTH the password and the hash.
PW=$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' </dev/urandom | head -c 32)
HASH=$(docker run --rm httpd:2.4-alpine htpasswd -bnBC 12 "" "$PW" | tr -d ':\n')
echo "length: ${#HASH}"   # must print 60
```

## The compose

Upstream's compose runs a second service, `collabora/code`, for editing Office documents. It is
an entire LibreOffice, it runs as root, it publishes another port, and its start command downloads
a stylesheet from a third-party gist every time it boots. It is dropped here, which cleanly
disables the office suite because that feature is off unless `OFFICE_URL` is set:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: machines/filestash@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:22fabc40»
    restart: always
    environment:
      APPLICATION_URL: "${FILESTASH_PUBLIC_HOST}"
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
    ports:
      - "8334:8334"
    volumes:
      - filestash-state:/app/data/state/

volumes:
  filestash-state:
```

`FILESTASH_PUBLIC_HOST` is the bare dname, no scheme, and it has to match exactly or every page
outside `/admin` is refused. `FILESTASH_ADMIN_BCRYPT` is the 60-character hash. Note what is
absent: no `CANARY` (it appears nowhere in the source), no office server, no database.

## Proving it is claimed and closed

Run this once the deploy reports ready.

The gate here is unusually strong, because `/healthz` is registered with no middleware at all and
its body reports the result of a configuration sanity check. A `pass` proves the app is running,
that it can read its config, **and** that the admin hash is the right length. redu's hostname
answers 502 for the first couple of minutes, and this script exits `2 INCONCLUSIVE` rather than
passing whenever it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Filestash is not an open admin console.
#   ./verify-filestash.sh filestash-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN (fix it now), 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -u
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-filestash.sh <hostname>}"
H=$(mktemp); S=$(mktemp); C=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$H" "$S" "$C"' EXIT
XHR='X-Requested-With: XmlHttpRequest'

# 1. GATE. /healthz needs no headers and checks the config as well as the process.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$H" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/healthz")
case "$code" in
  502|503|504) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: proxy answered $code, the container is probably still starting. Re-run in two minutes."; exit 2 ;;
  200) : ;;
  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /healthz answered $code."; exit 2 ;;
esac
if ! grep -q '"status"' "$H"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 but no status key. That is not Filestash answering."
  exit 2
fi
if grep -q '"status": *"transcient"' "$H"; then
  echo "FAIL the configuration sanity check is failing. Body:"
  cat "$H"; echo
  echo "     An admin.auth size that is not 60 means ADMIN_PASSWORD holds a plaintext password"
  echo "     rather than a bcrypt hash. Nobody can administer this instance. Redeploy with a hash."
  exit 1
fi
grep -q '"status": *"pass"' "$H" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected /healthz body: $(cat "$H")"; exit 2; }
echo "OK   /healthz says pass: [REDACTED:value] app is up, its config is readable, and the admin hash is 60 chars."

# 2. OWNERSHIP. Ask the question that actually matters: can an ANONYMOUS caller read the config?
#    Do NOT use /admin/api/session for this. Its result field is tagged omitempty, so the healthy
#    answer (false) is omitted from the JSON entirely, and a script testing for its absence would
#    read a refused request as a pass. This endpoint has three distinguishable outcomes instead,
#    and none of them is an absence:
#      a "result" key      -> the whole configuration came back. The instance is OPEN.
#      "Permission Denied" -> AdminOnly refused us. That is the state we want.
#      "Not Allowed"       -> SecureOrigin refused us, i.e. the XHR header did not arrive.
#                             That proves nothing about ownership, so it is INCONCLUSIVE.
sc=$(curl -sS -o "$S" -w '%{http_code}' -H "$XHR" "https://$HOST/admin/api/config")
grep -q '"status"' "$S" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /admin/api/config answered $sc with no status key, so this proved nothing."
  exit 2
}
if grep -q '"result"' "$S"; then
  echo "FAIL an ANONYMOUS caller just read the entire configuration, which means auth.admin is"
  echo "     empty. The same caller can POST it back and own the instance. Take this down now."
  exit 1
fi
if grep -qi 'Not Allowed' "$S"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: refused by the origin check, not by the admin check. The X-Requested-With"
  echo "             header did not reach the app, so ownership was never tested. Fix and re-run."
  exit 2
fi
grep -qi 'Permission Denied' "$S" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected refusal from /admin/api/config: $(cat "$S")"
  exit 2
}
echo "OK   an anonymous caller is refused with Permission Denied, so ADMIN_PASSWORD took effect."

# 3. THE FRONT DOOR. auth is [] exactly when no identity provider is configured.
cc=$(curl -sS -o "$C" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/config")
[ "$cc" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/config answered $cc."; exit 2; }
grep -q '"connections"' "$C" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/config has no connections key."; exit 2; }
nauth=$(python3 -c 'import json,sys
d=json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
print(len((d.get("result") or d).get("auth") or []))' "$C")
if [ "$nauth" = "0" ]; then
  echo "FAIL no authentication middleware is configured, so the connect form is open to anyone."
  echo "     They cannot read your files, but they CAN make this server dial any host they name."
  echo "     Set middleware.identity_provider.type to admin before handing this URL over."
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK   an authentication middleware is configured: the connect form asks for a password first."

# 4. Prove the OUTCOME, not the status code: the admin password must actually sign in. A 60-char
#    hash in the right place still fails to log in if it hashes a different password. With
#    Accept: application/json this endpoint returns an access token in the body, so assert on that.
if [ -n "${FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-}" ]; then
  A=$(mktemp)
  printf '{"password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD" \
    | curl -sS -o "$A" -H "$XHR" -H 'accept: application/json' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
      --data-binary @- "https://$HOST/admin/api/session" >/dev/null
  if grep -q 'access_token' "$A"; then
    echo "OK   the admin password signs in and returns a token."
  else
    echo "FAIL the admin password does NOT sign in. The stored hash and this password disagree."
    echo "     Body: $(cat "$A")"
    rm -f "$A"; exit 1
  fi
  rm -f "$A"
else
  echo "note set FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD to also prove the password signs in. Do it before finishing."
fi
```

Bodies go in on stdin rather than in the argument list, because an argument is visible in `ps` to
every user on the machine.

## What it does not do

It does not store your files. Filestash is a front end: it holds a configuration, some share links
and a search index, and everything else lives on the storage you point it at. That is why there is
no database here, why the volume is small, and why deleting the deployment cannot lose your
documents.

## Licence, since it is a fair question

Filestash is AGPL v3, unmodified. Self-hosting it for yourself or your team is squarely permitted.
Section 13 is the clause worth knowing: because it is offered to others over a network, whoever
operates the instance owes its users an offer of the source of the version they run. The stock
image satisfies that by pointing at the upstream repository, and because there are no version tags,
record the digest you deployed so you can say precisely which version that was.

Deploying it does not make redu the operator: the instance is yours, in your own account.

## Deploy log

- Not yet deployed. The first real run replaces this line with its measured time, flavor and hourly
  rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong. The three most useful things it
  can add are a memory figure, since upstream publishes none, a straight answer on whether m1.small
  would have been enough, and confirmation that the admin authentication middleware can be set
  through the API exactly as this file claims rather than only through the console.

# Self-host Filestash on redu

One web file manager in front of all your storage: SFTP, FTP, S3, WebDAV, Git, Dropbox, Google
Drive. One small Go container, a volume, a public HTTPS URL, and no database at all.

## What this deploys

- **Filestash** from the official image, pinned by digest, on one m1.medium VM, port 8334.
- A named volume on `/app/data/state/`, which holds the configuration, the signing secret and
  the SQLite files behind share links and search.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
- **No database.** Filestash keeps its own state on the volume, and your files stay where they
  already are.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Filestash on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Read this part before you deploy it anywhere

A **stock Filestash is an unauthenticated admin console.** That is not a bug report, it is what the
code says: the middleware that guards the admin API wraps its entire check inside "if an admin
password is set". With no admin password, an anonymous request can read the whole configuration and
write it back, including setting the admin password to its own.

Filestash is in this library, and changedetection.io was researched and dropped, for one reason:
Filestash has an environment variable that closes this **before the process ever listens.** So this
recipe is built around two steps that are not optional:

1. **`ADMIN_PASSWORD` at deploy time**, which settles who owns the console.
2. **The admin authentication middleware, set the moment the container is healthy**, which settles
   who can reach the connect form at all.

Without the second one, an anonymous visitor cannot read your files, but they can make your server
open outbound connections to any host they name, which is a probe into your own private network and
a free relay out of it.

## The password is a hash, not a password

This one has cost people their instance. `ADMIN_PASSWORD` is stored **verbatim** and compared
with `bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword`. Filestash normally hashes in the browser, on the setup page.
So the variable must contain a **bcrypt hash**, and a plaintext password produces an instance that
nobody, including you, can ever administer: the comparison can never match, and because the value
is non-empty the setup page is gone.

Upstream agrees, in its own health check, which flags the config whenever the stored value is not
exactly 60 characters. That is the length of a bcrypt hash.

```bash
# Generate one without installing anything. Keep BOTH the password and the hash.
PW=$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' </dev/urandom | head -c 32)
HASH=$(docker run --rm httpd:2.4-alpine htpasswd -bnBC 12 "" "$PW" | tr -d ':\n')
echo "length: ${#HASH}"   # must print 60
```

## The compose

Upstream's compose runs a second service, `collabora/code`, for editing Office documents. It is
an entire LibreOffice, it runs as root, it publishes another port, and its start command downloads
a stylesheet from a third-party gist every time it boots. It is dropped here, which cleanly
disables the office suite because that feature is off unless `OFFICE_URL` is set:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: machines/filestash@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:22fabc40»
    restart: always
    environment:
      APPLICATION_URL: "${FILESTASH_PUBLIC_HOST}"
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
    ports:
      - "8334:8334"
    volumes:
      - filestash-state:/app/data/state/

volumes:
  filestash-state:
```

`FILESTASH_PUBLIC_HOST` is the bare dname, no scheme, and it has to match exactly or every page
outside `/admin` is refused. `FILESTASH_ADMIN_BCRYPT` is the 60-character hash. Note what is
absent: no `CANARY` (it appears nowhere in the source), no office server, no database.

## Proving it is claimed and closed

Run this once the deploy reports ready.

The gate here is unusually strong, because `/healthz` is registered with no middleware at all and
its body reports the result of a configuration sanity check. A `pass` proves the app is running,
that it can read its config, **and** that the admin hash is the right length. redu's hostname
answers 502 for the first couple of minutes, and this script exits `2 INCONCLUSIVE` rather than
passing whenever it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Filestash is not an open admin console.
#   ./verify-filestash.sh filestash-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN (fix it now), 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -u
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-filestash.sh <hostname>}"
H=$(mktemp); S=$(mktemp); C=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$H" "$S" "$C"' EXIT
XHR='X-Requested-With: XmlHttpRequest'

# 1. GATE. /healthz needs no headers and checks the config as well as the process.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$H" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/healthz")
case "$code" in
  502|503|504) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: proxy answered $code, the container is probably still starting. Re-run in two minutes."; exit 2 ;;
  200) : ;;
  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /healthz answered $code."; exit 2 ;;
esac
if ! grep -q '"status"' "$H"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 but no status key. That is not Filestash answering."
  exit 2
fi
if grep -q '"status": *"transcient"' "$H"; then
  echo "FAIL the configuration sanity check is failing. Body:"
  cat "$H"; echo
  echo "     An admin.auth size that is not 60 means ADMIN_PASSWORD holds a plaintext password"
  echo "     rather than a bcrypt hash. Nobody can administer this instance. Redeploy with a hash."
  exit 1
fi
grep -q '"status": *"pass"' "$H" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected /healthz body: $(cat "$H")"; exit 2; }
echo "OK   /healthz says pass: [REDACTED:value] app is up, its config is readable, and the admin hash is 60 chars."

# 2. OWNERSHIP. Ask the question that actually matters: can an ANONYMOUS caller read the config?
#    Do NOT use /admin/api/session for this. Its result field is tagged omitempty, so the healthy
#    answer (false) is omitted from the JSON entirely, and a script testing for its absence would
#    read a refused request as a pass. This endpoint has three distinguishable outcomes instead,
#    and none of them is an absence:
#      a "result" key      -> the whole configuration came back. The instance is OPEN.
#      "Permission Denied" -> AdminOnly refused us. That is the state we want.
#      "Not Allowed"       -> SecureOrigin refused us, i.e. the XHR header did not arrive.
#                             That proves nothing about ownership, so it is INCONCLUSIVE.
sc=$(curl -sS -o "$S" -w '%{http_code}' -H "$XHR" "https://$HOST/admin/api/config")
grep -q '"status"' "$S" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /admin/api/config answered $sc with no status key, so this proved nothing."
  exit 2
}
if grep -q '"result"' "$S"; then
  echo "FAIL an ANONYMOUS caller just read the entire configuration, which means auth.admin is"
  echo "     empty. The same caller can POST it back and own the instance. Take this down now."
  exit 1
fi
if grep -qi 'Not Allowed' "$S"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: refused by the origin check, not by the admin check. The X-Requested-With"
  echo "             header did not reach the app, so ownership was never tested. Fix and re-run."
  exit 2
fi
grep -qi 'Permission Denied' "$S" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected refusal from /admin/api/config: $(cat "$S")"
  exit 2
}
echo "OK   an anonymous caller is refused with Permission Denied, so ADMIN_PASSWORD took effect."

# 3. THE FRONT DOOR. auth is [] exactly when no identity provider is configured.
cc=$(curl -sS -o "$C" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/config")
[ "$cc" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/config answered $cc."; exit 2; }
grep -q '"connections"' "$C" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/config has no connections key."; exit 2; }
nauth=$(python3 -c 'import json,sys
d=json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
print(len((d.get("result") or d).get("auth") or []))' "$C")
if [ "$nauth" = "0" ]; then
  echo "FAIL no authentication middleware is configured, so the connect form is open to anyone."
  echo "     They cannot read your files, but they CAN make this server dial any host they name."
  echo "     Set middleware.identity_provider.type to admin before handing this URL over."
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK   an authentication middleware is configured: the connect form asks for a password first."

# 4. Prove the OUTCOME, not the status code: the admin password must actually sign in. A 60-char
#    hash in the right place still fails to log in if it hashes a different password. With
#    Accept: application/json this endpoint returns an access token in the body, so assert on that.
if [ -n "${FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-}" ]; then
  A=$(mktemp)
  printf '{"password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD" \
    | curl -sS -o "$A" -H "$XHR" -H 'accept: application/json' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
      --data-binary @- "https://$HOST/admin/api/session" >/dev/null
  if grep -q 'access_token' "$A"; then
    echo "OK   the admin password signs in and returns a token."
  else
    echo "FAIL the admin password does NOT sign in. The stored hash and this password disagree."
    echo "     Body: $(cat "$A")"
    rm -f "$A"; exit 1
  fi
  rm -f "$A"
else
  echo "note set FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD to also prove the password signs in. Do it before finishing."
fi
```

Bodies go in on stdin rather than in the argument list, because an argument is visible in `ps` to
every user on the machine.

## What it does not do

It does not store your files. Filestash is a front end: it holds a configuration, some share links
and a search index, and everything else lives on the storage you point it at. That is why there is
no database here, why the volume is small, and why deleting the deployment cannot lose your
documents.

## Licence, since it is a fair question

Filestash is AGPL v3, unmodified. Self-hosting it for yourself or your team is squarely permitted.
Section 13 is the clause worth knowing: because it is offered to others over a network, whoever
operates the instance owes its users an offer of the source of the version they run. The stock
image satisfies that by pointing at the upstream repository, and because there are no version tags,
record the digest you deployed so you can say precisely which version that was.

Deploying it does not make redu the operator: the instance is yours, in your own account.

## Deploy log

- Not yet deployed. The first real run replaces this line with its measured time, flavor and hourly
  rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong. The three most useful things it
  can add are a memory figure, since upstream publishes none, a straight answer on whether m1.small
  would have been enough, and confirmation that the admin authentication middleware can be set
  through the API exactly as this file claims rather than only through the console.

Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.
⛔ NEVER WRITE A CREDENTIAL INTO redu.md. It is committed and read by the next person and the next agent. Names of variables, yes; their values, never. Hand secrets to the user in the session instead.

plan_deploy OVER-SIZES A PULLED COMPOSE STACK. Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. Show the user the plan, but size from the app's real memory figure when you have one.

THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. SSH is still yours for everything else - a shell on a real machine is the point, not a fallback. ⭐ MEASURED over 38 deploys: of 241 ssh escapes, 146 (61%) were exactly these four things, and the four tools were called 11 times. They are faster than a login, they cost the VM nothing extra (the reading is already cached), and reaching for ssh to run `docker ps` is the single most common wasted minute in a deploy.

⛔ THE PRIMARY SURFACE'S HOSTNAME COMES FROM THE TOP-LEVEL dname, NOT FROM expose[0].dname, WHICH IS SILENTLY DISCARDED. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. Measured at the protocol level, HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with the subprotocol echoed back. ⚠️ TEST IT WITH `curl --http1.1`: plain curl negotiates HTTP/2, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all, so the app answers as an ordinary GET and the failure looks exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. Browsers use HTTP/1.1 for websockets regardless. Do not disable an app's realtime features on the strength of an HTTP/2 curl.

---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/mickael-kerjean/filestash
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: machines/filestash pinned by digest (there are no version tags)
  port: 8334
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: none. Filestash keeps its own state in SQLite files on a volume, and the FILES live on whatever storage you point it at.
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0278
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: filestash
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: NOBODY, UNLESS YOU SET ADMIN_PASSWORD, AND UNTIL YOU DO, EVERY ANONYMOUS REQUEST IS ALREADY AN ADMIN. This is the reason this entry exists in the shape it does, so read it before anything else. server/middleware/session.go:29-56, the AdminOnly middleware, wraps its ENTIRE check in an if statement that only runs when auth.admin is non-empty. With no admin password the middleware calls the handler with no check at all, and routes.go:40-47 puts GET /admin/api/config, POST /admin/api/config, the workflow CRUD and the audit log behind exactly that middleware. So on a fresh instance anyone can READ the whole configuration, including the secret key and any stored credentials, and WRITE it, including setting the admin password to their own. server/ctrl/admin.go:16-20 confirms it from the other side: GET /admin/api/session returns true when auth.admin is empty. And static.go:49,80 redirects every page to the setup form, so the app actively shows a stranger the door. There is no wizard token and no first-visitor lock. ADMIN_PASSWORD is the ONLY thing that closes this, and cmd/main.go:26-46 applies it during InitConfig, several steps before the listener binds. NEVER deploy this without it."
  - "⛔⛔ ADMIN_PASSWORD MUST CONTAIN A BCRYPT HASH, NOT A PASSWORD, AND GETTING IT WRONG LOCKS YOU OUT FOREVER WITH NO ERROR. config.go:242-246 stores the environment value verbatim through ConfigElement.Set (:429-444), which does no hashing; the hashing normally happens in the BROWSER at public/assets/pages/adminpage/ctrl_setup.js:91. Every login then runs bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword against the stored string. Put a plaintext password in and the comparison can never succeed, while auth.admin is non-empty so the setup page is gone and the admin console is unreachable by anybody including you. Upstream asserts the same rule in its own health check: server/ctrl/report.go:73-75 flags the config when auth.admin is not exactly 60 characters, which is the length of a bcrypt hash. Generate one, for example with a throwaway container: run htpasswd -bnBC 12 with an empty username inside httpd:2.4-alpine and strip the leading colon and the newline. golang.org/x/crypto v0.54.0 bcrypt.go:265-279 accepts $2a$, $2b$ and $2y$ alike, so an htpasswd hash is fine. THEN PROVE IT: the /healthz check below tells you the length is right, and signing in proves the password matches. Do both."
  - "⛔⛔ CLOSE THE FRONT DOOR TOO, AND DO IT AS THE FIRST STEP AFTER BOOT. ADMIN_PASSWORD settles who owns the admin console; it does nothing about the connect form on the home page. middleware.identity_provider.type defaults to EMPTY (server/ctrl/session.go:192-203), and config/config.json ships seven connectors: WebDav, FTP, SFTP, GIT, S3, Dropbox and Drive. So an anonymous visitor cannot read YOUR files, they have no credentials, but they can make YOUR server open outbound connections to any host they name. That is an SSRF probe into the user's own private network and a free egress relay, and it is the same class of problem that got changedetection.io dropped from this library. The fix is upstream's own admin authentication plugin (server/plugin/plg_authenticate_admin/index.go), which redirects visitors to a password page where only the admin password is accepted. Set middleware.identity_provider.type to admin through POST /admin/api/config immediately after the container is healthy, BEFORE you hand the URL over, and verify it with the anonymous check below. If the user wants a genuinely public file browser, that is a decision to take with them, not a default to leave in place."
  - "⛔ EVERY SCRIPTED CALL TO THE ADMIN API NEEDS THE HEADER X-Requested-With: XmlHttpRequest, AND WITHOUT IT THE FAILURE LOOKS LIKE AN AUTH FAILURE. server/middleware/http.go:94-100, inside SecureOrigin, lets a request through only when that header is present, or when features.api.enable is true AND the request carries no cookies; otherwise it logs Intrusion detection and returns ErrNotAllowed. routes.go:35-47 puts the whole admin API behind SecureOrigin. So a plain curl to /admin/api/session gets refused, which reads exactly like a wrong password and will send you hunting the bcrypt hash instead of the header. Add the header to every admin call, and gate your script on a well-formed response body rather than on a status code."
  - "⛔ DO NOT WRITE A CHECK AGAINST /admin/api/session, BECAUSE ITS HEALTHY ANSWER IS AN ABSENCE. server/common/response.go:13-16 tags the field as Result interface{} with json:\"result,omitempty\", so SendSuccessResult(res, false) encodes to a body with NO result key at all. The correctly-locked instance therefore answers {status: ok} and nothing else, which is indistinguishable from a request that was refused before it reached the handler. A script that reads 'no result: true present' as a pass would pass on a 502, on a missing header, and on a typo in the hostname. Probe GET /admin/api/config instead: it has three outcomes that can be told apart, a result key means the config came back and the instance is OPEN, Permission Denied means AdminOnly refused you which is what you want, and Not Allowed means SecureOrigin refused you so the test never ran. Both refusals are HTTP 403, so it is the MESSAGE that distinguishes them (server/common/error.go:17-18)."
  - "⛔ APPLICATION_URL MUST BE EXACTLY THE PUBLIC HOSTNAME, AND SETTING IT WRONG BREAKS EVERYTHING EXCEPT /admin. config.go:247-250 maps it onto general.host, and SecureOrigin (http.go:81-92) then refuses any request whose Host header does not match, with the single exception of paths starting /admin/. That exception is a kindness, not a bug: it is how you get back in and fix it. Generate the dname yourself UP FRONT in full filestash-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form and pass that; a bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match. The value is the bare host, no scheme."
  - "⛔ DELETE THE wopi_server SERVICE. Upstream's compose runs collabora/code beside the app, and on redu it is all cost and no benefit: it is an entire LibreOffice, many times the size of Filestash itself, it publishes port 9980, it runs as user: root, its aliasgroup1 is the wildcard https://.*:443, and its command curls a stylesheet from a third-party GitHub gist on EVERY start, which is both a boot-time dependency on somebody else's server and a supply-chain hook. Drop it and leave OFFICE_URL unset: plg_editor_wopi/config.go:10-24 defaults features.office.enable to FALSE unless OFFICE_URL is set, so this is a clean disable rather than a break. What you lose is in-browser editing of Word, Excel and PowerPoint documents. Everything else, including browsing, uploading, downloading, image and video preview, and the text and code editors, is unaffected. If a user genuinely needs office editing, that is a second VM sized for LibreOffice, not a container squeezed onto this one."
  - "⛔ THERE IS NO VERSION TO PIN, SO PIN THE DIGEST. The Docker Hub repository machines/filestash carries 310 tags and not one of them is a version: the only current tag is latest, rebuilt 2026-08-16, and the rest are 2023-era git shas plus the oddities lowa, trial and a latest-amd64 from 2025-06-30. GitHub publishes no releases either. So reaching for the rolling tag is not laziness here, it is the only tag there is, which is exactly why it must not go in a recipe: it moves under you and a redeploy silently crosses however many months of changes. Pin machines/filestash@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:22fabc40», which was the latest manifest on 2026-08-17. Upgrading means reading the new digest yourself and deciding to move; there is no changelog to read first, so treat an upgrade as a change with a rollback plan."
  - "⛔ MOUNT A VOLUME ON /app/data/state/ OR EVERY REDEPLOY IS A FACTORY RESET. This is the whole product state: constants.go:20-26 puts config under state/config (including the admin hash, the secret key and any configured connections), certificates under state/certs, plugins under state/plugins, SQLite databases under state/db, the search index under state/search and logs under state/log. server/model/index.go:15 and four widget plugins open SQLite files in state/db for share links, workflows, metadata, chat and recents. This is NOT the silent-SQLite-fallback trap the rest of this library warns about: Filestash has no other mode, the SQLite is deliberate, and the volume IS the answer. ⚠️ Note that TMP_PATH is cache/, OUTSIDE state/, and constants.go:53 wipes it at boot, which is correct and is why it is not on the volume. Use a NAMED volume rather than a bind mount into the project directory, because a source re-upload replaces that directory. A fresh named volume is seeded from the image, which already ships a default config.json and is chowned to the filestash user by docker/Dockerfile:37, so there is no permission dance."
  - "THE SECRET THAT A REDEPLOY DESTROYS IS general.secret_key, AND THERE IS NO ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE FOR IT. config.go:251-255 generates it as a 16-character random string on first boot and writes it into config.json, and constants.go:71-77 derives the admin cookie key, the user session key, the hash key and the signature key from it. Lose it and every admin session, every user session and every share-link proof stops verifying; anything encrypted in the config stops decrypting. Because it lives in the config file rather than the environment, THE VOLUME IS THE THING YOU PROTECT, which is the same sentence as the quirk above and is why that one is not optional. There is a related variable, CONFIG_SECRET: [REDACTED:value] it and the encrypted config paths (the identity-provider and attribute-mapping params) are keyed from it instead of from general.secret_key (config_state.go:43-47,84). Setting it means one fewer thing living only on the volume; changing it later makes those two fields undecryptable. Decide once."
  - "⛔ DO NOT PUT STORAGE CREDENTIALS INTO A PRE-CONFIGURED CONNECTION. # Self-host Filestash on redu

One web file manager in front of all your storage: SFTP, FTP, S3, WebDAV, Git, Dropbox, Google
Drive. One small Go container, a volume, a public HTTPS URL, and no database at all.

## What this deploys

- **Filestash** from the official image, pinned by digest, on one m1.medium VM, port 8334.
- A named volume on `/app/data/state/`, which holds the configuration, the signing secret and
  the SQLite files behind share links and search.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
- **No database.** Filestash keeps its own state on the volume, and your files stay where they
  already are.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Filestash on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Read this part before you deploy it anywhere

A **stock Filestash is an unauthenticated admin console.** That is not a bug report, it is what the
code says: the middleware that guards the admin API wraps its entire check inside "if an admin
password is set". With no admin password, an anonymous request can read the whole configuration and
write it back, including setting the admin password to its own.

Filestash is in this library, and changedetection.io was researched and dropped, for one reason:
Filestash has an environment variable that closes this **before the process ever listens.** So this
recipe is built around two steps that are not optional:

1. **`ADMIN_PASSWORD` at deploy time**, which settles who owns the console.
2. **The admin authentication middleware, set the moment the container is healthy**, which settles
   who can reach the connect form at all.

Without the second one, an anonymous visitor cannot read your files, but they can make your server
open outbound connections to any host they name, which is a probe into your own private network and
a free relay out of it.

## The password is a hash, not a password

This one has cost people their instance. `ADMIN_PASSWORD` is stored **verbatim** and compared
with `bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword`. Filestash normally hashes in the browser, on the setup page.
So the variable must contain a **bcrypt hash**, and a plaintext password produces an instance that
nobody, including you, can ever administer: the comparison can never match, and because the value
is non-empty the setup page is gone.

Upstream agrees, in its own health check, which flags the config whenever the stored value is not
exactly 60 characters. That is the length of a bcrypt hash.

```bash
# Generate one without installing anything. Keep BOTH the password and the hash.
PW=$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' </dev/urandom | head -c 32)
HASH=$(docker run --rm httpd:2.4-alpine htpasswd -bnBC 12 "" "$PW" | tr -d ':\n')
echo "length: ${#HASH}"   # must print 60
```

## The compose

Upstream's compose runs a second service, `collabora/code`, for editing Office documents. It is
an entire LibreOffice, it runs as root, it publishes another port, and its start command downloads
a stylesheet from a third-party gist every time it boots. It is dropped here, which cleanly
disables the office suite because that feature is off unless `OFFICE_URL` is set:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: machines/filestash@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:22fabc40»
    restart: always
    environment:
      APPLICATION_URL: "${FILESTASH_PUBLIC_HOST}"
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
    ports:
      - "8334:8334"
    volumes:
      - filestash-state:/app/data/state/

volumes:
  filestash-state:
```

`FILESTASH_PUBLIC_HOST` is the bare dname, no scheme, and it has to match exactly or every page
outside `/admin` is refused. `FILESTASH_ADMIN_BCRYPT` is the 60-character hash. Note what is
absent: no `CANARY` (it appears nowhere in the source), no office server, no database.

## Proving it is claimed and closed

Run this once the deploy reports ready.

The gate here is unusually strong, because `/healthz` is registered with no middleware at all and
its body reports the result of a configuration sanity check. A `pass` proves the app is running,
that it can read its config, **and** that the admin hash is the right length. redu's hostname
answers 502 for the first couple of minutes, and this script exits `2 INCONCLUSIVE` rather than
passing whenever it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this Filestash is not an open admin console.
#   ./verify-filestash.sh filestash-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = closed, 1 = OPEN (fix it now), 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -u
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-filestash.sh <hostname>}"
H=$(mktemp); S=$(mktemp); C=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$H" "$S" "$C"' EXIT
XHR='X-Requested-With: XmlHttpRequest'

# 1. GATE. /healthz needs no headers and checks the config as well as the process.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$H" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/healthz")
case "$code" in
  502|503|504) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: proxy answered $code, the container is probably still starting. Re-run in two minutes."; exit 2 ;;
  200) : ;;
  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /healthz answered $code."; exit 2 ;;
esac
if ! grep -q '"status"' "$H"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 but no status key. That is not Filestash answering."
  exit 2
fi
if grep -q '"status": *"transcient"' "$H"; then
  echo "FAIL the configuration sanity check is failing. Body:"
  cat "$H"; echo
  echo "     An admin.auth size that is not 60 means ADMIN_PASSWORD holds a plaintext password"
  echo "     rather than a bcrypt hash. Nobody can administer this instance. Redeploy with a hash."
  exit 1
fi
grep -q '"status": *"pass"' "$H" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected /healthz body: $(cat "$H")"; exit 2; }
echo "OK   /healthz says pass: [REDACTED:value] app is up, its config is readable, and the admin hash is 60 chars."

# 2. OWNERSHIP. Ask the question that actually matters: can an ANONYMOUS caller read the config?
#    Do NOT use /admin/api/session for this. Its result field is tagged omitempty, so the healthy
#    answer (false) is omitted from the JSON entirely, and a script testing for its absence would
#    read a refused request as a pass. This endpoint has three distinguishable outcomes instead,
#    and none of them is an absence:
#      a "result" key      -> the whole configuration came back. The instance is OPEN.
#      "Permission Denied" -> AdminOnly refused us. That is the state we want.
#      "Not Allowed"       -> SecureOrigin refused us, i.e. the XHR header did not arrive.
#                             That proves nothing about ownership, so it is INCONCLUSIVE.
sc=$(curl -sS -o "$S" -w '%{http_code}' -H "$XHR" "https://$HOST/admin/api/config")
grep -q '"status"' "$S" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /admin/api/config answered $sc with no status key, so this proved nothing."
  exit 2
}
if grep -q '"result"' "$S"; then
  echo "FAIL an ANONYMOUS caller just read the entire configuration, which means auth.admin is"
  echo "     empty. The same caller can POST it back and own the instance. Take this down now."
  exit 1
fi
if grep -qi 'Not Allowed' "$S"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: refused by the origin check, not by the admin check. The X-Requested-With"
  echo "             header did not reach the app, so ownership was never tested. Fix and re-run."
  exit 2
fi
grep -qi 'Permission Denied' "$S" || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: unexpected refusal from /admin/api/config: $(cat "$S")"
  exit 2
}
echo "OK   an anonymous caller is refused with Permission Denied, so ADMIN_PASSWORD took effect."

# 3. THE FRONT DOOR. auth is [] exactly when no identity provider is configured.
cc=$(curl -sS -o "$C" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/config")
[ "$cc" = "200" ] || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/config answered $cc."; exit 2; }
grep -q '"connections"' "$C" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /api/config has no connections key."; exit 2; }
nauth=$(python3 -c 'import json,sys
d=json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
print(len((d.get("result") or d).get("auth") or []))' "$C")
if [ "$nauth" = "0" ]; then
  echo "FAIL no authentication middleware is configured, so the connect form is open to anyone."
  echo "     They cannot read your files, but they CAN make this server dial any host they name."
  echo "     Set middleware.identity_provider.type to admin before handing this URL over."
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK   an authentication middleware is configured: the connect form asks for a password first."

# 4. Prove the OUTCOME, not the status code: the admin password must actually sign in. A 60-char
#    hash in the right place still fails to log in if it hashes a different password. With
#    Accept: application/json this endpoint returns an access token in the body, so assert on that.
if [ -n "${FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-}" ]; then
  A=$(mktemp)
  printf '{"password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD" \
    | curl -sS -o "$A" -H "$XHR" -H 'accept: application/json' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
      --data-binary @- "https://$HOST/admin/api/session" >/dev/null
  if grep -q 'access_token' "$A"; then
    echo "OK   the admin password signs in and returns a token."
  else
    echo "FAIL the admin password does NOT sign in. The stored hash and this password disagree."
    echo "     Body: $(cat "$A")"
    rm -f "$A"; exit 1
  fi
  rm -f "$A"
else
  echo "note set FILESTASH_ADMIN_PASSWORD to also prove the password signs in. Do it before finishing."
fi
```

Bodies go in on stdin rather than in the argument list, because an argument is visible in `ps` to
every user on the machine.

## What it does not do

It does not store your files. Filestash is a front end: it holds a configuration, some share links
and a search index, and everything else lives on the storage you point it at. That is why there is
no database here, why the volume is small, and why deleting the deployment cannot lose your
documents.

## Licence, since it is a fair question

Filestash is AGPL v3, unmodified. Self-hosting it for yourself or your team is squarely permitted.
Section 13 is the clause worth knowing: because it is offered to others over a network, whoever
operates the instance owes its users an offer of the source of the version they run. The stock
image satisfies that by pointing at the upstream repository, and because there are no version tags,
record the digest you deployed so you can say precisely which version that was.

Deploying it does not make redu the operator: the instance is yours, in your own account.

## Deploy log

  rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong. The three most useful things it
  can add are a memory figure, since upstream publishes none, a straight answer on whether m1.small
  would have been enough, and confirmation that the admin authentication middleware can be set
  through the API exactly as this file claims rather than only through the console.
